questions.q: In a Conditional Access policy, what is a "grant control"?
options: The named location or device platform the policy checks before it fires
The list of cloud apps the policy is assigned to
What a user must satisfy to be let in once the policy's assignments and conditions match, such as MFA or a compliant device
A log entry showing how a past sign-in was evaluated
questions.explain: Grant controls are the requirements — MFA, compliant device, hybrid join, approved app, or block — that apply once a policy's assignments and conditions match a sign-in.

questions.q: Which of the following is an "assignment" in a Conditional Access policy, as distinct from a condition or a control?
options: Specifying which users, groups, or cloud apps (including workload identities) the policy applies to
Requiring sign-in frequency to be re-evaluated every hour
Requiring the device to be marked compliant
The sign-in risk level reported by Identity Protection
questions.explain: Assignments define who and what the policy targets — users/groups, cloud apps, and workload identities. Risk level is a condition, and compliant-device/sign-in-frequency are controls.

questions.q: A tenant has Policy A (requires MFA for User X) and Policy B (requires a compliant device for User X), and both match a given sign-in. What actually happens?
options: Entra ID picks whichever policy was created first and ignores the other
The user only has to satisfy whichever policy has the stricter name
The policies cancel each other out and the sign-in is blocked automatically
Both grant controls apply together — the user needs MFA and a compliant device
questions.explain: Entra ID evaluates every matching policy and requires all of their grant controls to be satisfied — it never selects a single "best match" policy.

questions.q: What specifically makes a break-glass emergency access account actually effective during a misconfigured Conditional Access rollout?
options: Giving it the Global Reader role instead of Global Administrator, to limit blast radius
Explicitly excluding it from every Conditional Access policy that could block it
Syncing it from on-premises Active Directory so it stays consistent with other admin accounts
Requiring it to pass the same compliant-device check as every other admin account
questions.explain: A break-glass account only works as a true fallback if it is excluded from the policies that could lock it out; it should also be cloud-only, not synced from on-prem AD.

questions.q: What does report-only mode actually do when applied to a new Conditional Access policy?
options: Logs what the policy would have done against real sign-ins — success, failure, or not-applicable — without enforcing it
Immediately blocks any sign-in the policy would have blocked, but without notifying the user
Applies the policy only to Global Administrator accounts as a safety test
Disables the policy entirely until an administrator manually re-enables it
questions.explain: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against real sign-in traffic and records the outcome in the sign-in logs, letting you validate it before switching it to On.
